topic: Gupta golden age II — mixed tiers
description: Chandragupta II, Samudragupta, Nalanda university roots, mathematics, art, decline

questions.stem: The famous IRON PILLAR of Delhi (in the Qutb complex) bears an inscription dating it to the time of which Gupta ruler?

options.option_text: Samudragupta, the Napoleon of India by V.A. Smith
Chandra (most likely Chandragupta II 'Vikramaditya')
Skandagupta, who repulsed the Hunas in the 5th century
Kumaragupta, who founded the Nalanda university

questions.explanation: Iron Pillar — at Mehrauli (Qutb complex), Delhi. Bears a Sanskrit inscription in Brahmi script praising King Chandra (most scholars identify as Chandragupta II, r. ~375-415 CE, also called 'Vikramaditya'). 7+ m tall, ~6 tonnes, near-pure wrought iron, has resisted rust for ~1600 years (high P content + dense protective oxide layer). Originally erected at Vishnupada near Udayagiri / Mathura, moved to Delhi by Anangpal Tomar (~10th-11th c.) or earlier. Demonstrates ancient Indian metallurgical excellence.

questions.stem: The court of CHANDRAGUPTA II is famously associated with NINE GEMS, including the great Sanskrit poet:

options.option_text: Tulsidas, author of the Ramcharitmanas
Kalidasa, author of Shakuntala and Meghaduta
Banabhatta, author of the Harshacharita
Ravidasa, the Bhakti saint of Varanasi

questions.explanation: KALIDASA — greatest poet-dramatist of classical Sanskrit, often associated with Chandragupta II's Navaratnas. Major works: ABHIJÑĀNAŚHĀKUNTALAM (recognition of Shakuntala — Goethe's lifelong favourite), MEGHADUTA (cloud messenger), MĀLAVIKĀGNIMITRAM, RAGHUVAMSHA, KUMARASAMBHAVA. Other 'gems': Varahamihira (astronomer), Dhanvantari (medicine), Vararuchi (grammar), etc. Distractor 1 — Tulsidas was 16th c. (Mughal era). Distractor 3 — Banabhatta was at Harsha's court (7th c.). Distractor 4 — Ravidas was 15th-16th c. Bhakti saint.

questions.stem: ARYABHATA, the great Indian mathematician-astronomer who lived during the Gupta era, is credited with:

options.option_text: Composing the Vedas, the oldest scriptures of India
Approximating π and proposing earth's rotation on its axis
Drafting the Arthashastra of Mauryan statecraft
Writing the Charaka Samhita on traditional medicine

questions.explanation: ARYABHATA (476-550 CE) — wrote ARYABHATIYA (499 CE) at age 23. Achievements: gave π ≈ 3.1416 (very accurate); explained that the Earth rotates on its axis (causing apparent celestial motion) — anticipating Copernicus by 1000 years; correctly explained eclipses (lunar = moon in earth's shadow; solar = moon between sun + earth) without supernatural causes; trigonometric tables (sine ≈ jya). India's first satellite (1975) named ARYABHATA in his honour. Distractor 1 = Vedic seers, much older. Distractor 3 = Kautilya / Chanakya. Distractor 4 = Charaka (medicine, separate field).

questions.stem: The Chinese Buddhist pilgrim FA-HIEN (Faxian) visited India during the reign of:

options.option_text: Samudragupta, the conqueror-king of north India
Chandragupta II Vikramaditya around 405-411 CE
Harshavardhana of the Pushyabhuti dynasty later
Ashoka the Great of the Mauryan empire much earlier

questions.explanation: Fa-Hien (Faxian, 337-422 CE) — Chinese Buddhist monk; visited India 399-414 CE, during Chandragupta II's reign. Wrote 'Foguoji' (A Record of Buddhist Kingdoms). Praised Indian society as peaceful + prosperous; few capital punishments. Visited Buddhist sites — Lumbini, Bodh Gaya, Sarnath, Kushinagar, Pataliputra. Other Chinese visitors: HIUEN-TSANG / Xuanzang (629-645 CE) during HARSHA's reign; I-TSING (671-695 CE) during the late Gupta / early imperial decline.

questions.stem: The decimal place-value system and the concept of ZERO as a number were systematised in India during which period?

options.option_text: The Mauryan period under Ashoka the Great
The Gupta and post-Gupta period (roughly 4th-7th c. CE)
The Vedic period of pre-Buddha sacred literature
The Mughal period under Akbar's court patronage

questions.explanation: Zero as a number + place-value notation — developed in India during the Gupta + post-Gupta era. Brahmagupta (628 CE, 'Brahmasphutasiddhanta') gave first systematic rules for ZERO and NEGATIVE numbers. Aryabhata used place-value implicitly. Bakhshali manuscript (~3rd-4th c. or later) contains the earliest known dot-symbol for zero. The 'Indo-Arabic numerals' (1, 2, 3, ..., 9, 0) were transmitted to the Arab world (al-Khwarizmi, ~825 CE) and from there to Europe (Fibonacci, ~1200 CE) — revolutionising mathematics. Distractor 1 — too early. Distractor 3 — Vedic math used a base-10 system but no formal zero. Distractor 4 — too late.

questions.stem: The decline of the Gupta empire in the 5th-6th century CE was accelerated by repeated invasions of which Central Asian people?

options.option_text: The Mongols under Genghis Khan and his successors
The Hunas (White Huns / Hephthalites) from beyond the Hindu Kush
The Greeks under Alexander the Great's successors only
The Mughals from Central Asia later in the 16th century

questions.explanation: HUNAS (Hephthalites / White Huns) — invaded India from across the Hindu Kush mountains, late 5th c. CE. SKANDAGUPTA (455-467 CE) defeated them initially. But repeated waves under MIHIRAKULA + TORAMANA (early 6th c.) damaged the empire's western provinces (Punjab, Malwa). Combined with internal weak succession + economic strain → Gupta empire fragmented by mid-6th c. Distractor 1 — Mongols came in the 13th c. (Chinggis, then Ilkhans, finally Mughals). Distractor 3 — Greeks came at the time of Alexander (327 BCE) — much earlier. Distractor 4 — Mughals are 16th c.

questions.stem: NALANDA UNIVERSITY — one of the world's earliest residential universities — was founded in the:

options.option_text: 1st century BCE under the Mauryan dynasty
5th century CE under Kumaragupta I of the Gupta dynasty
10th century CE under the Pala dynasty in Bengal
12th century CE under the Delhi Sultanate

questions.explanation: Nalanda Mahavihara — founded c. 5th c. CE under KUMARAGUPTA I (~427 CE). Continued patronage by later Gupta + Pala kings. At its peak: ~10,000 students, 2,000 teachers, 9-storey library 'Dharmaganja'. Subjects: Buddhism, Vedas, logic, grammar, medicine, astronomy. Visited by Hiuen Tsang (early 7th c.) who studied here for years. SACKED + BURNED by BAKHTIYAR KHILJI (~1193 CE), library destroyed. UNESCO World Heritage Site (2016). Modern Nalanda University (2014) revived as international university near the ancient site.
